learn.title: A shorter name for a type
learn.body: `typedef` gives an existing type a new name. With structs it saves you from writing `struct` every time. Instead of `struct point`, you can just say `point`. It does not create a new kind of data, only a name.

learn.title: Typedef and an array
learn.body: This prints `Ana is 31` and then `Bo is 27`. The name `person` is now a type. A `char` array field holds the name, and the array of two persons sits in one row of memory.

learn.title: Structs on the heap
learn.body: `malloc` works with any type. Use `sizeof *p`, set a name with `strcpy` (a name cannot be assigned with `=`), and use `->`. This prints `Ana 31`. Free the block when done.

learn.title: Reading a typedef
learn.body: `typedef struct { char name[12]; int age; } person;`
steps: `person p;` makes a variable of that type

learn.body: The name text must fit in the array. A 12-byte array holds up to 11 letters plus the ending 0, so never copy a longer string into it.

choices: Gives a type a new name
questions.explanation: It only adds a name for a type that already exists.

questions.prompt: After the typedef, you can declare `\_\_ p;` using the new type.
questions.explanation: `person` is now a type name, so `person p;` works.

questions.prompt: How do you set a `char name[12]` field to "Ana"?
questions.explanation: Arrays cannot be assigned with `=`, so copy the characters in.

questions.prompt: What does the first program print for the first person? Write the full line.
questions.explanation: It prints the name, then the text, then the age.

questions.prompt: A `char name[12]` field can hold at most how many letters?
questions.explanation: One byte is needed for the ending 0.

questions.prompt: What must you do with the struct from `malloc`?
questions.explanation: Heap blocks, including structs, need a `free`.

questions.prompt: Match the code to what it does.
questions.explanation: Everything you learned about arrays and pointers works for structs.
